messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Frank is a sixty-year-old warehouse worker who lives with his partner in a quiet suburban town. He served in the Vietnam War, and the memory that haunts him most is an ambush in a village near the DMZ: his squad was pinned down, two of his closest friends were killed within minutes, and he escaped only by crawling through a ditch while enemy fire shredded the air around him. For decades he told himself he had simply been lucky, but he never believed it. He felt certain, with a conviction that had settled into his bones, that he should not have made it out alive. That belief—that he should not have survived—kept the ambush close to the surface, priming it to intrude into his mind without warning. This survival guilt became the lens through which he saw everything: the world felt permanently unsafe, and the man he had been before the war—the confident young soldier, the brother, the son—seemed like a stranger he could no longer recognize.

In the years after his discharge, Frank’s conviction that the world is a dangerous place shaped nearly every decision he made. He avoided any location that reminded him of the ambush—wooded areas, narrow alleyways, even the back corner of the warehouse where dust and shadows pooled, because they felt too close to the cover he had hidden in. At work he found himself steering clear of that section of the floor, taking longer routes to the loading dock, and never explaining why. When his well-meaning partner once bought him a green jacket that resembled an old field jacket, he could not bring himself to wear it. The guilt and the sense that he no longer knew himself made it unbearable to see his own reflection in anything that connected him to that past. And yet the past had a way of forcing its way in. On bad nights, without warning, the memory would surface—not as a story he could tell, but as the same raw terror, the same choking guilt. He tried to find words to describe it to his partner once, but the sounds would not come; his mouth went dry and he sat in silence, unable to shape what he saw in his mind. Those moments of remembering always returned him to the core belief that he should have died, that the world had no place for someone like him, and that the man he used to be was gone forever.

Because the memory brought such terror and guilt, Frank learned to avoid thinking about the ambush altogether. He kept his mind busy with repetitive tasks at the warehouse—stacking boxes, counting inventory—so that his thoughts would not drift. He changed the subject whenever anyone mentioned the war, and he refused to watch any movie or news report that showed combat. But the avoidance came at a cost. With each distance he created from the event, he felt more disconnected from his own history and from the person he had been. He told himself that if he could just keep the memory locked away, he could function, but he also came to believe that he no longer had a real identity, only a shell that went to work and came home. The more he avoided, the more his guilt and his sense of lost self grew, feeding a cycle that he could not name but could feel tightening around him like a slow weight.

Now, after a recent episode in the warehouse—when a sudden loud noise made him drop to the ground, trembling, in front of his coworkers—Frank’s partner urged him to seek help. He agreed, but he is terrified of what talking might bring back. He is most afraid that if he lets himself remember fully, he will be swallowed by the same guilt and terror, and that there will be nothing left of the person he already feels he has lost.
